## BST: Height and Data {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

BST operations depend on the **height** ($h$) of the tree.

But we want to analyze in terms of **$n$** (the amount of data).

So we need relationships between $h$ and $n$:

- $h \geq$ \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
- $h \leq$ \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
Fill in:
- h >= log₂(n) (lower bound — best case, perfectly balanced)
- h <= n - 1 (upper bound — worst case, degenerate)

Lower bound is good news (fast operations). Upper bound is bad news (slow operations).
:::

## Average Case

The height of a BST depends on the **order** data is inserted.

How many different insertion orders for $n$ keys? \_\_\_\_\_

Average height, over all arrangements of $n$ keys: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: {.fragment}
| Operation | Avg Case | Worst Case |
|-----------|----------|------------|
| find | $\Theta(\log n)$ | $\Theta(n)$ |
| insert | $\Theta(\log n)$ | $\Theta(n)$ |
| delete | $\Theta(\log n)$ | $\Theta(n)$ |
:::

::: notes
- n! different insertion orders
- Average height is O(log n) — this was proven by Reed (2003)
- But worst case is still O(n), and real-world data is often nearly sorted!
:::

## Comparing Dictionary Implementations

| Structure | Insert | Find | Delete | Sorted Iterate |
|-----------|--------|------|--------|----------------|
| Unsorted list | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n log n) |
| Sorted list | O(n) | O(log n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Hash table | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | Not possible |
| BST  | O(\_\_\_\_) | O(\_\_\_\_) | O(\_\_\_\_) | O(n) |

::: notes
BST answers are O(height) — which is O(log n) average, O(n) worst case.
:::

## Why Trees Instead of Hash Tables?

Hash tables give O(1) expected time. Why use trees?

Trees can do things hash tables can't:

- **Sorted iteration**: Traverse keys in order
- **Range queries**: Find all keys between A and B
- **Predecessor/successor**: Find the next-smallest key
- **No hash function needed**: Works with any comparable type

The **height balance** of a tree $T$ is: $b = \text{height}(T_R) - \text{height}(T_L)$

A tree $T$ is **height balanced** if:

- \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

- \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
Fill in:
- |b| ≤ 1 for every node in the tree
- Both subtrees are also height balanced (recursive!)

Equivalently: every node has balance factor in {-1, 0, 1}.
:::

Lead students to articulate: "balanced" — left and right subtrees are about the same height. Then formalize on next slide.

## Rotations on a BST {.smaller}

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 500 290" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width: 500px;">
  <!-- Edges -->
  <line x1="250" y1="30" x2="130" y2="90" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="250" y1="30" x2="370" y2="90" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="130" y1="90" x2="70" y2="150" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="130" y1="90" x2="190" y2="150" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="370" y1="90" x2="310" y2="150" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="370" y1="90" x2="430" y2="150" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="430" y1="150" x2="400" y2="210" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="430" y1="150" x2="470" y2="210" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="470" y1="210" x2="445" y2="270" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>

  <!-- Nodes -->
  <circle cx="250" cy="30" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="250" y="37" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">50</text>

  <circle cx="130" cy="90" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="130" y="97" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">30</text>

  <circle cx="370" cy="90" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="370" y="97" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">80</text>

  <circle cx="70" cy="150" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="70" y="157" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">20</text>

  <circle cx="190" cy="150" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="190" y="157" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">40</text>

  <circle cx="310" cy="150" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="310" y="157" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">60</text>

  <circle cx="430" cy="150" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="430" y="157" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">90</text>

  <circle cx="400" cy="210" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="400" y="217" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">85</text>

  <circle cx="470" cy="210" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="470" y="217" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">99</text>

  <circle cx="445" cy="270" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="445" y="277" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">95</text>
</svg>
```


::: notes
Balance factors: 50 (b=2), 30 (b=0), 80 (b=2), 20 (b=0), 40 (b=0), 60 (b=0), 90 (b=1), 85 (b=0), 99 (b=-1), 95 (b=0).

Lowest unbalanced node is 80 (b=+2). Its right child 90 has b=+1 → right-right (outer) case → single left rotation at 80. Annotate the rotation on the board.

After left rotation at 80: 90 replaces 80, 80 becomes 90's left child, 85 moves to become 80's right child. Result: balanced!
:::

## Rotations on a BST {.smaller}

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 380 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width: 380px;">
  <!-- Edges -->
  <line x1="200" y1="30" x2="100" y2="90" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="200" y1="30" x2="300" y2="90" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="100" y1="90" x2="50" y2="150" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="100" y1="90" x2="150" y2="150" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="150" y1="150" x2="190" y2="210" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>

  <!-- Nodes -->
  <circle cx="200" cy="30" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="200" y="37" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">70</text>

  <circle cx="100" cy="90" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="100" y="97" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">40</text>

  <circle cx="300" cy="90" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="300" y="97" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">80</text>

  <circle cx="50" cy="150" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="50" y="157" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">20</text>

  <circle cx="150" cy="150" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="150" y="157" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">50</text>

  <circle cx="190" cy="210" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="190" y="217" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">60</text>
</svg>
```

::: notes
b=-2 at 70, left child 40 has b=+1 (right-heavy). This is a zig-zag (left-right / inner case). Try a single right rotation at 70: 40 becomes root, 70 becomes right child, 50 moves to 70's left child. Result: 40(20, 70(50(_, 60), 80)) — still b=+2 at 40! The single rotation just moved the problem. We need a double rotation.

The fix (left-right double rotation):
Step 1: Left rotate at 40 → 70(50(40(20), 60), 80)
Step 2: Right rotate at 70 → 50(40(20), 70(60, 80))
Now balanced!
:::

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 380 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width: 380px;">
  <!-- Edges -->
  <line x1="200" y1="30" x2="100" y2="90" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>

  <line x1="100" y1="90" x2="150" y2="150" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="150" y1="150" x2="190" y2="210" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/>

  <!-- Nodes -->
  <circle cx="200" cy="30" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="200" y="37" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">70</text>

  <circle cx="100" cy="90" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="100" y="97" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">40</text>

  <circle cx="300" cy="90" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="300" y="97" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">80</text>

  <circle cx="50" cy="150" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="50" y="157" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">20</text>

  <circle cx="150" cy="150" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="150" y="157" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">50</text>

  <circle cx="190" cy="210" r="18" fill="#27ae60"/>
  <text x="190" y="217" text-anchor="middle" fill="black">60</text>
</svg>
```

::: notes
b=-2 at 70, left child 40 has b=+1 (right-heavy). This is a zig-zag (left-right / inner case). Try a single right rotation at 70: 40 becomes root, 70 becomes right child, 50 moves to 70's left child. Result: 40(20, 70(50(_, 60), 80)) — still b=+2 at 40! The single rotation just moved the problem. We need a double rotation.

The fix (left-right double rotation):
Step 1: Left rotate at 40 → 70(50(40(20), 60), 80)
Step 2: Right rotate at 70 → 50(40(20), 70(60, 80))
Now balanced!
:::


## Operations on BSTs — Rotations {.smaller}

Rotation properties:

- There are **4 kinds**: left, right, left-right, right-left
- **Local** operations (subtrees not affected)
- **Constant time** ($O(1)$)
- **BST property maintained**

## AVL Trees {.smaller}

**GOAL**: use rotations to maintain balance of BSTs.

These trees have a special name: **AVL Trees**

Named after **A**delson-**V**elsky and **L**andis (1962).

**AVL Property**: For every node, $|b| \leq 1$.

Three issues to consider in the implementation:

1. Rotation
2. Maintaining height
3. Detecting imbalance

## Balanced Trees in Practice

| Language | Balanced Tree |
|----------|---------------|
| C++ | `std::map`, `std::set` (Red-Black) |
| Java | `TreeMap`, `TreeSet` (Red-Black) |
| Python | `sortedcontainers.SortedDict` (3rd party) |
| Databases | B-trees, B+ trees |

Python's built-in `dict` uses hash tables, not trees.

## Summary: Balanced Trees

1. **BST operations are O(height)** — height matters!

2. **Unbalanced BSTs can have O(n) height** — bad for sorted input

3. **Rotations** reshape BSTs while preserving order

4. **AVL trees** use rotations to maintain $|b| \leq 1$ for every node

5. **Diagnosing**: check child's balance factor to pick the rotation

6. **Guarantee**: O(log n) height, so O(log n) operations
